newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing judge denies media access petition.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing judge denies media access petition.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing case on Thursday rejected pleas from more than 50 news organisations to open up secret conferences with laywers that decide which jurors to dismiss in the trial of Timothy McVeigh.

U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch cited concerns about juror security, and added that he did not want prospective jurors to read news reports of how a person might be excused from serving on the jury.

Several prospective jurors questioned so far have expressed reservations about serving, citing such reasons as economic hardship and opposition to the death penalty. Only one person has been excused publicly from consideration -- a woman with a history of stress attacks.

The decision to maintain the daily secret conferences came on the fourth day of jury selection. McVeigh was accused of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, which killed 168 people and injuring hundreds of others.
The April 19, 1995 attack ranks as the worst domestic bombing on American soil, and the case has generated intense media coverage.

Media lawyer Tom Kelley told the judge that the public's interest in the case demanded that the closed-door meetings be shifted to open court. But the judge disagreed, saying he would unseal the proceedings at a later date and that should satisfy the public interest.
A car painter, a social worker, a stagehand expert in staging theatrical explosions and two grandmothers were among the 20 prospective jurors questioned so far.

They were questioned in open court by the judge, prosecutors and attorneys for McVeigh on their attitudes about the death penalty and on how much exposure they have had to pre-trial publicity. Their identities were kept secret and they were seated behind a wooden panel so that spectators in the courtroom could not see them.

Each morning the judge and the lawyers met in closed session to review the jurors that had been interviewed on the previous day. At that time lawyers could challenge certain potential jurors, citing specific reasons why those people should be dismissed.

McVeigh's chief attorney Stephen Jones argued that the reasons why a potential juror was challenged must be kept secret in case the challenge were denied. Otherwise, that person could end up sitting on the jury knowing an attorney did not want him there.
Opening up the challenge process would also disclose to potential panellists how to get off a jury, Jones said.
The jury selection process has moved slowly, with attorneys laboriously trying to get potential jurors to disclose their attitudes and knowledge of the case.
The 12 jurors and six alternates who are eventually chosen will have to be willing to at least consider sentencing McVeigh to death.

McVeigh officially was on trial for the "use of a weapon of mass destruction" and the murder of eight federal officials. A second defendant, his former Army buddy Terry Nichols, will be tried separately later. Both have pleaded not guilty.

Two prospective jurors said their religious beliefs would not allow them to vote for the death penalty. One philosophy teacher said he had very serious reservations about state executions. But the rest have said said they favour using the death penalty, although they have expressed different levels of support for it.
